headline: Second Beach Blues Run Hot, Beavertail Bass Wait for Dark
subhead: Bunker blitzes are hitting the ocean beaches on schedule while the rocky shore's bass have gone strictly nocturnal — here's where to fish both.
body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Beavertail Tuesday morning with the sun barely up and watched a school of peanut bunker get pushed right up against the ledge, so thick the water looked like it was boiling from underneath. That's the tell this time of year — when the bait starts pinning itself against structure at first light, something's pushing it, and out here in late July that something is almost always bluefish. Sure enough, ten minutes later the blues came through and it was game on for about twenty minutes before they pushed off toward the point.

That's been the pattern all week from Newport down through Sakonnet. We said the bunker-driven blitz would keep marching up the coast, and it has — Second Beach and the stretch off Sakonnet Point have both had daytime blitz windows this week, usually on the front half of the outgoing when bait gets squeezed against the beach or pinned on a rip. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, half-ounce Deadly Dicks — are getting bit the second they land if you're in the right spot at the right tide. The trick is timing. These blitzes don't linger. I've had fifteen-minute windows produce a dozen blues to eight pounds, then nothing but empty water for two hours. If you see birds working tight over bait near the rocks, don't wait — get a cast in before the whole thing slides down the beach.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Inshore surface temps are sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range, and that's put the bass on a strict nighttime schedule. Daytime, they're down deep on structure — the ledges off Beavertail, the rips under the Newport Bridge, the east passage current seams off Jamestown — just holding tight and not doing much. Wait for dark and they wake up. Eels drifted on the current seams off Beavertail and Fort Wetherill from an hour before high through the top of the tide have been the most consistent producer I've heard about, with a few schoolies mixed with some better fish pushing 30 inches. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in the Sakonnet River channel after dark are doing the same job for guys who don't want to fuss with live eels. Daytime bass fishing on the south shore right now is mostly a waste of gas unless you're working deep water with jigs right on bottom.

Fluke have softened up in the shallow spots the way they usually do once the water gets this warm — the open flats inside the Sakonnet and off Second Beach have gone quiet. The better fish are sliding into the deeper current, Charlestown Breachway and the channel out front of Watch Hill Reef, where the water keeps moving and stays a few degrees cooler. Four-inch white Gulp on quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb through Charlestown, has been picking at keepers mixed with a lot of shorts. Not a banner week for fluke, but honest work if you put in the drift time.

Scup are everywhere on the ledges right now and they're the easy button if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating — squid strips or sandworms on a hi-lo rig right on the rocks at Beavertail or the Jamestown bridge pilings will fill a cooler fast, and there's nothing wrong with that on a hot afternoon.

Tog guys, I know you're itching — I've had three separate conversations this week about which cracks are holding fish. Season's closed until August 1st here, so for now it's scouting only. I've been easing crabs down into a few spots off Beavertail and the Jamestown side just to confirm what's home, and there's fish there. When the season flips open next week, start on the slack around the new moon tides — dead low or dead high, whichever gives you the cleanest drift-free window — and work green crabs tight to the base of the ledges in 15 to 25 feet. I'll have specifics once I've had a proper crack at it.

On the albie front — nothing yet, and I want to be straight about that instead of hyping something that isn't here. It's still a touch early for the south shore breachways; that push usually doesn't show at Napatree, Watch Hill, or Weekapaug until the back half of August into September when the bay anchovies and silversides really thicken up in the current. I have been seeing more silversides pushing through Napatree on the outgoing this week than I did two weeks ago, which is the kind of early signal I look for. Worth keeping a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig in the bag if you're out there working bluefish, but I wouldn't plan a trip around albies just yet.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August and that ought to sharpen up current in the breachways and around Beavertail, which should help both the night bass bite and eventually tip off the albie arrival. If the wind stays out of the south and the ocean holds the moderate chop it's had — a few feet at five seconds, nothing dangerous but enough to keep the surf stirred — I'd stick with the early-morning and dusk blitz windows on the beaches, save the bulk of my bass effort for after dark on the ledges, and start easing into the breachways with the light albie gear as August gets closer.
